 What if we stayed on daylight saving time all winter along the Gulf Coast? 
 By Matt Barrentine Published : Oct. 28, 2026 at 10:47 AM CDT | Updated : 4 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google MOBILE, Ala. ( WALA ) - As we prepare to turn our clocks back an hour on Nov. 1, many people along the Mobile-Pensacola Gulf Coast will be asking the same question: What if we just stayed on daylight saving time all winter? The biggest difference would be brighter evenings, but that extra hour of afternoon sunlight would come at the expense of darker mornings.
 Take Thanksgiving, for example. Under our current system, the sun sets in Mobile around 4:50 p.m. by late November. If we stayed on daylight saving time, sunset would shift to around 5:50 p.m. That could mean more daylight for an afternoon walk, some backyard football or a little extra time outside before sitting down for Thanksgiving dinner. The trade-off? Sunrise would be closer to 7:30 a.m., rather than around 6:30 a.m. under standard time.
 Christmas would bring a similar change. Instead of sunset arriving around 4:50 p.m. in late December, daylight would stretch until roughly 5:50 p.m. That extra evening light could make it easier to enjoy Christmas decorations, visit family or get outside after work. However, children heading to school and adults commuting early would face darker mornings, with sunrise approaching 7:45 a.m. around Christmas.
 The important thing to remember is that staying on daylight saving time would not give us more daylight. The sun would still follow the same seasonal pattern, with our shortest days occurring around the winter solstice in December. We would simply shift an hour of daylight from the morning to the evening.
 So, would permanent daylight saving time be better for the Mobile-Pensacola area? It depends on your routine. If you enjoy outdoor activities after work or want more light for holiday gatherings, brighter evenings might be appealing. If you prefer driving to work or school after sunrise, standard time has the advantage. Either way, the debate isn’t really about gaining sunlight — it’s about deciding when we want to use it.
